title: Jacobian criterion for smoothness of a relative global complete intersection at a prime
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n,c\ge0$ integers and $f_1,\dots,f_c\in R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] such that $S=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_c)$ is a relative global complete intersection [def-weil-pbc-relative-global-complete-intersection]. For a subset $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ of cardinality $c$ let $g_I=\det(\partial f_j/\partial x_i)_{j=1,\dots,c,\ i\in I}\in R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ (the determinant [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] of the $c\times c$ matrix with rows indexed by $j$ and columns by the elements of $I$ in increasing order, $\partial/\partial x_i$ the formal partial derivatives [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]) and $\bar g_I\in S$ its image. Let $\mathfrak q\subset S$ be a prime ideal. Then $R\to S$ is smooth at $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-singular-ideal] if and only if there is a subset $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $|I|=c$ and $\bar g_I\notin\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00TE (lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-smooth, line 37629) and its proof (naive cotangent complex of a relative global complete intersection, Lemma 00SV lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal; Lemma 00S7 lemma-localize-NL; maximal minors)

proof.text: (The naive cotangent complex of the presentation.) Put $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, $K=(f_1,\dots,f_c)$ (we write $K$ for the ideal, as $I$ denotes a set of indices), so $S=P/K$, and write $\bar p$ for the image in $S$ of $p\in P$. By [lem-weil-pbc-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal-free] the $S$-module $K/K^2$ is free [def-weil-pbc-free-module] with basis $\varepsilon_j=f_j\bmod K^2$, $j=1,\dots,c$. The $S$-linear map $\mathrm d:K/K^2\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^nS\,\mathrm dx_i$, $\mathrm d(p\bmod K^2)=\sum_i\overline{\partial p/\partial x_i}\,\mathrm dx_i$ (the map of [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-localization-conormal-split], whose ideal is called $I$ there) sends $\varepsilon_j\mapsto\sum_i\overline{\partial f_j/\partial x_i}\,\mathrm dx_i$, so in the bases $(\varepsilon_j)$ and $(\mathrm dx_i)$ it is given by the $n\times c$ matrix $M$ over $S$ [def-weil-matrix] with $M_{ij}=\overline{\partial f_j/\partial x_i}$ [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]. For $I=\{i_1<\dots<i_c\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ let $M_I$ be the $c\times c$ submatrix [def-weil-submatrix] of $M$ formed by the rows $i_1,\dots,i_c$, so $(M_I)_{kj}=\overline{\partial f_j/\partial x_{i_k}}$. Then $\det M_I=\bar g_I$: (a) $\det$ is given by the formula $\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_kN_{\sigma(k),k}$ [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], a polynomial with integer coefficients in the entries, so every ring homomorphism (here $P\to S$; below also $S\to S_g$ and isomorphisms of polynomial rings) commutes with $\det$ applied entrywise; (b) $M_I$ is the transpose of the image of the matrix $(\partial f_j/\partial x_{i_k})_{j,k}$ defining $g_I$, and $\det N^{\mathsf T}=\det N$, since substituting $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^{-1}$ in the formula turns $\prod_kN_{k,\sigma(k)}=\prod_kN_{\sigma^{-1}(k),k}$ into the terms of $\det N$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ (sgn is a homomorphism to $\{\pm1\}$). This is Stacks' remark that the maximal minors of the matrix of the naive cotangent complex are the $g_I$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00TE (lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-smooth, lines 37644-37670), first paragraph, with Lemma Tag 00SV (lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal) part (3)

proof.text: ('Only if': a left inverse over $S_g$.) Assume $R\to S$ is smooth at $\mathfrak q$. By [def-weil-pbc-singular-ideal] there is $g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$ such that the localization $S_g$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] is a smooth $R$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map]. By [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-localization-conormal-split] (with its ideal $K$, $A=S=P/K$, $a=g$) the localized map $\mathrm d_g:(K/K^2)_g\to\bigoplus_iS_g\,\mathrm dx_i$ [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away] has an $S_g$-linear left inverse $\lambda$. The $S_g$-module $(K/K^2)_g$ is free with basis $\varepsilon_j/1$: every element is $m/g^e$ with $m=\sum_js_j\varepsilon_j$ (step 1), so equals $\sum_j(s_j/g^e)(\varepsilon_j/1)$; and if $\sum_j(s_j/g^e)(\varepsilon_j/1)=0$ then $g^k\sum_js_j\varepsilon_j=0$ in $K/K^2$ for some $k$, so $g^ks_j=0$ for all $j$ by freeness, i.e. $s_j/g^e=0$ in $S_g$. In the bases $(\varepsilon_j/1)$ and $(\mathrm dx_i)$, $\mathrm d_g$ has the matrix $M^{(g)}=(M_{ij}/1)$, the image of $M$ in $S_g$, and $\lambda$ has a $c\times n$ matrix $B$ over $S_g$; $\lambda\circ\mathrm d_g=\mathrm{id}$ reads $BM^{(g)}=1_{c\times c}$ (composition of linear maps between finite free modules is the product of their matrices).

proof.text: ('Only if': a maximal minor outside $\mathfrak q$.) By [lem-weil-pbc-matrix-left-inverse-minors] (2), applied over the ring $S_g$ to the $n\times c$ matrix $M^{(g)}$ ($n\ge c$ by step 3), $f=1$ and the matrix $B$ of step 2 with $BM^{(g)}=1\cdot1_{c\times c}$, we get $1=1^c=\sum_{|I|=c}b_I\det(M^{(g)}_I)$ with $b_I\in S_g$. By step 1 (a), (b) applied to $P\to S\to S_g$, $\det(M^{(g)}_I)=\bar g_I/1$. Suppose $\bar g_I\in\mathfrak q$ for every $I$. Write $b_I=s_I/g^e$ with $s_I\in S$ and one $e$ for all $I$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. Then $1/1=(\sum_Is_I\bar g_I)/g^e$ in $S_g$, so $g^k(g^e-\sum_Is_I\bar g_I)=0$ in $S$ for some $k$, i.e. $g^{k+e}=\sum_Ig^ks_I\bar g_I\in\mathfrak q$, and $g\in\mathfrak q$ since $\mathfrak q$ is prime: a contradiction. Hence $\bar g_I\notin\mathfrak q$ for some $I$ with $|I|=c$. (Stacks argues with the rank of the matrix over $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$; the identity $1=\sum b_I\bar g_I/1$ is the same fact without passing to the residue field.)

proof.text: ('If': a presentation of $S_g$.) Assume $I=\{i_1<\dots<i_c\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $g:=\bar g_I\notin\mathfrak q$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-principal-localization-naive-cotangent] with $A=R$, $B=S$, $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, $\alpha:P\to S$ the quotient map (kernel $K=(f_1,\dots,f_c)$, called $I$ in that node) and the lift $f=g_I$ of $g$: the $R$-algebra map $\beta:P[y]\to S_g$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] equal to $\alpha$ followed by $S\to S_g$ on $P$ and with $\beta(y)=1/g$ is surjective, and its kernel $J$ is generated by $K$ and $g_Iy-1$, hence $J=(f_1,\dots,f_c,g_Iy-1)$. Identifying $P[y]$ with the polynomial ring $R[x_1,\dots,x_n,y]$ in $n+1$ variables [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], $\beta$ induces an isomorphism of $R$-algebras $R[x_1,\dots,x_n,y]/(f_1,\dots,f_c,g_Iy-1)\cong S_g$ sending $p\bmod J$ to $\beta(p)$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00TE (lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-smooth, lines 37644-37670), second paragraph ('the algebra S_g is smooth over R'), via the presentation of S_g of Lemma Tag 08JZ (lemma-principal-localization-NL)

proof.text: ('If': renaming the variables.) Since $I$ has $c$ elements, $c\le n$; let $j_1<\dots<j_{n-c}$ be the elements of $\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus I$. Let $\tau:R[z_1,\dots,z_{n+1}]\to R[x_1,\dots,x_n,y]$ be the $R$-algebra isomorphism of polynomial rings [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] induced by the bijection of variables $z_k\mapsto x_{i_k}$ ($k\le c$), $z_{c+1}\mapsto y$, $z_{c+1+l}\mapsto x_{j_l}$ ($1\le l\le n-c$), and put $F_j=\tau^{-1}(f_j)$ ($j\le c$), $F_{c+1}=\tau^{-1}(g_Iy-1)$. Then $\tau$ maps the ideal $(F_1,\dots,F_{c+1})$ onto $(f_1,\dots,f_c,g_Iy-1)$, so with step 5 we get an isomorphism of $R$-algebras $\alpha':R[z_1,\dots,z_{n+1}]/(F_1,\dots,F_{c+1})\cong S_g$, $p\bmod(F)\mapsto\beta(\tau(p))$. Moreover $\tau(\partial F/\partial z_k)=\partial\tau(F)/\partial v_k$ for every $F$, where $v_k=\tau(z_k)$ is the variable $z_k$ is sent to: both sides are $R$-linear in $F$ and agree on monomials by the explicit formula of [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative] ($\tau$ only renames exponents).

source.place: Algebra, proof of Lemma Tag 00TE (lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-smooth, lines 37644-37670), second paragraph; the renaming 'after renumbering the variables' is implicit in the source

proof.text: ('If': the Jacobian determinant is a unit.) Let $N=(\partial F_j/\partial z_k)_{1\le j,k\le c+1}$. By step 6, $\tau(N_{jk})=\partial f_j/\partial x_{i_k}$ for $j,k\le c$; $\tau(N_{j,c+1})=\partial f_j/\partial y=0$ for $j\le c$ ($f_j$ does not involve $y$); $\tau(N_{c+1,k})=y\,\partial g_I/\partial x_{i_k}$ for $k\le c$ (Leibniz rule, $\partial y/\partial x_{i_k}=0$); and $\tau(N_{c+1,c+1})=\partial(g_Iy-1)/\partial y=g_I$ ($g_I$ does not involve $y$) [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]. So $\tau(N)$ (entrywise) is block lower triangular with diagonal blocks $(\partial f_j/\partial x_{i_k})_{j,k\le c}$ and the $1\times1$ block $(g_I)$, and by [lem-weil-pbc-block-triangular-determinant] ($p=c$, $q=1$) and step 1 (a), $\tau(\det N)=\det\tau(N)=\det(\partial f_j/\partial x_{i_k})_{j,k}\cdot g_I=g_I^2$ [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Hence the image of $\det N$ under $R[z]\to R[z]/(F)\xrightarrow{\alpha'}S_g$ is $\beta(g_I^2)=(g/1)^2$, a unit of $S_g$ (inverse $1/g^2$). As $n+1\ge c+1\ge0$, $(n+1,\,c+1,\,F_1,\dots,F_{c+1},\,\alpha')$ is a standard smooth presentation of $S_g$ over $R$ [def-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-algebra] (the standard smooth definition uses $\det(\partial F_j/\partial z_k)$ over the first $c+1$ variables; its orientation is immaterial by step 1 (b)).

proof.text: ('If': conclusion.) By step 7 and [lem-weil-pbc-standard-smooth-is-smooth], $S_g$ is a smooth $R$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map]; since $g=\bar g_I\notin\mathfrak q$, $R\to S$ is smooth at $\mathfrak q$ by [def-weil-pbc-singular-ideal]. (This direction does not use that $S$ is a relative global complete intersection.) Together with steps 2-4 this proves the equivalence.

split_report.summary: Statement checked against Stacks 00TE and kept; the determinant now cites def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant (added to stmt_deps) and the orientation of the minor (rows j, columns I) is written. Proof in 8 steps after the proof of 00TE. Step 1: I/I^2 free on the f_j (new unsplit node for 00SV (3)) and the maximal minors of the matrix of d are the g_I (determinant commutes with ring maps and with transposition, written out). 'Only if' (steps 2-4): smooth at q gives g not in q with S_g smooth; lem-weil-pbc-smooth-localization-conormal-split gives a left inverse of the localized d, i.e. a matrix B with B M = 1 over S_g; S_g is nonzero and c <= n (Cauchy-Binet); lem-weil-pbc-matrix-left-inverse-minors (2) (07DQ) with f = 1 gives 1 = sum b_I g_I/1 in S_g, which forces some g_I outside q (replaces Stacks' rank over kappa(q)). 'If' (steps 5-8): S_g = R[x,y]/(f, g_I y - 1) by the existing 08JZ node, the variables renamed so x_I come first and y next; the (c+1)x(c+1) Jacobian is block lower triangular with determinant g_I^2, a unit in S_g, so S_g is standard smooth (00T6) hence smooth (00T7, Mathlib leaf), as the lead's brief suggested; this realizes Stacks' 'by construction quasi-isomorphic to a free module' through the standard smooth node instead of 00S7 directly. The 'if' direction does not need the complete intersection hypothesis.
